Validation: replicating the papers and agreement with pyfgls

Source: vignettes/validation.Rmd
validation.Rmd

The results below were precomputed (the Monte Carlo simulations take tens of minutes) by tools/replicate_tables.R and tools/compare_python_r.R in the source repository, and are stored in the package:

rep <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "replication.rds", package = "fgls"))
xl <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "cross_language.rds", package = "fgls"))
rep$replications
#>  pg26_table1 pg26_general  gp24_table1           s9 
#>         2000         1000         1000         1000

The papers use 10,000 replications; with 1,000 the Monte Carlo standard error of a coverage rate near 0.95 is about 0.007. The same designs are run, with tolerances, by the package’s acceptance tests (FGLS_SLOW_TESTS=true).

Perron and González-Coya (2026), Table 1

AR(1) errors (0.8), a regressor that responds to past innovations, \(T = 500\); slope estimates (true value 1):

knitr::kable(rep$pg26_table1, digits = 3)
estimator rmse bias paper_rmse paper_bias
OLS 0.399 0.395 0.399 0.395
Durbin 0.038 0.002 0.036 NA
GLS (infeasible) 0.024 0.000 0.025 NA
FGLS 0.027 0.001 0.025 0.001
Cochrane-Orcutt 0.041 0.031 0.041 0.031
rho (FGLS) 0.034 -0.008 0.034 -0.008
rho (CO) 0.174 -0.170 NA -0.171 
rep$pg26_table1_median_k
#> [1] 1

OLS is inconsistent, Cochrane-Orcutt is biased (its estimate of \(\rho\) is biased downwards), and FGLS matches the infeasible GLS.

Perron and González-Coya (2026), Tables 2–5 (selected cells)

The robust intervals have close to nominal coverage for all \(\gamma\); the naive ones under-cover when the regressor is not exogenous (\(\gamma > 0\)).

González-Coya and Perron (2024), Table 1

Empirical MSE of the adaptive-Lasso FGLS slope relative to OLS, \(T = 400\), with the paper’s values, and coverage of the eq. (6)+(8) intervals:

knitr::kable(rep$gp24_table1, digits = 3)
skedastic T emse_ratio paper_ratio coverage
homoskedastic 400 1.010 1.000 0.957
x 400 0.905 0.920 0.953
x2 400 0.687 0.700 0.955
log2 400 0.449 0.460 0.945
exp 400 0.443 0.450 0.955
step 400 0.728 0.735 0.954

At \(T = 100\)–\(200\) the ratios of this implementation (and of pyfgls) are a few hundredths above the paper’s; the T = 400 column is matched.

AR(1) 0.5, homoskedastic 0.937 0.535 0.542 0.963 0.958 0.076 0.075

F-CH improves on F-C under heteroskedasticity and loses nothing under homoskedasticity. With 1,000 replications some F-CH coverage rates are slightly above 0.95; the intervals are conservative, not too short.

Agreement with pyfgls

fgls is a port of the Python package pyfgls. Both packages fitted the same 500 data sets per design with the same cross-validation folds (pyfgls 0.1.0):

s <- xl$summary
s <- s[s$quantity %in% c("beta", "se", "kstar", "selected", "coverage_95"), ]
knitr::kable(s, digits = 15, row.names = FALSE)
design quantity max_abs median_abs max_rel share_different
serial_ar1_nonexog beta 2.000000e-15 0e+00 2.000000e-15 0.000
serial_ar1_nonexog se 0.000000e+00 0e+00 1.000000e-15 0.000
serial_ar1_nonexog kstar 0.000000e+00 0e+00 0.000000e+00 0.000
serial_ar1_nonexog coverage_95 0.000000e+00 NA NA NA

Serial-correlation quantities agree to rounding error, and the selected AR order is identical in every data set. In about 1% of the Lasso data sets the degrees of freedom differ by one, because pyfgls 0.1.0 counts coefficients of order \(10^{-17}\) (left by interpolating its Lasso path at a knot) as selected. With the fixes proposed to pyfgls, everything agrees and the selected sets are identical:

xl$pyfgls_pr2$version
#> [1] "0.1.0 + emiliogcs/pyfgls#2"
knitr::kable(xl$pyfgls_pr2$summary, digits = 15, row.names = FALSE)
design max_rel share_support_different
serial_ar1_nonexog 2.300000e-14 NA
serial_ar2_exog 1.673000e-12 NA
serial_ma1 5.974939e-08 NA
hetero_log2 1.621900e-11 0
hetero_exp 1.521700e-11 0
combined_ar1_log2 3.056000e-12 0
combined_ar1_exp 3.445600e-11 0
combined_ar2_x2 7.462000e-12 0

The deterministic parts are also checked against golden fixtures generated by pyfgls (tests/testthat/test-golden-*.R), to relative precision \(10^{-8}\) or better.
